content: Perinatal mortality, also known as perinatal death, refers to the death of a fetus or a newborn and is used to calculate the perinatal mortality rate. There are variations in how perinatal mortality is defined, particularly regarding whether early fetal deaths and late neonatal deaths are included. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines perinatal mortality as deaths occurring during late pregnancy (at 22 completed weeks of gestation or more), during childbirth, and up to seven completed days of life. However, this definition is not universally accepted. Perinatal mortality is the combined total of fetal mortality and neonatal mortality. Fetal mortality refers to stillbirths or fetal deaths, which include any death of a fetus after 20 weeks of gestation or weighing 500 grams or more. In some definitions of perinatal mortality, early fetal deaths (occurring between 20 and 27 weeks of gestation) are excluded, and only late fetal deaths and neonatal deaths are included. Fetal deaths can be further categorized into deaths occurring before labor, known as antenatal (or antepartum) deaths, and deaths occurring during labor, referred to as intranatal (or intrapartum) deaths. Fetal mortality can be reduced by ensuring good preconception health in women before they become pregnant. Neonatal mortality refers to the death of a live-born infant. Early neonatal mortality is defined as the death of a newborn within the first seven days of life, while late neonatal mortality refers to deaths occurring after the seventh day but before the 29th day of life. The total neonatal mortality includes both early and late neonatal deaths. Some definitions of perinatal mortality include only early neonatal deaths. Neonatal mortality is influenced by the quality of medical care provided to the newborn in healthcare facilities. Neonatal mortality, along with postneonatal mortality (which covers deaths occurring in the remaining 11 months of the first year of life), contributes to the overall infant mortality rate. The perinatal mortality rate (PNMR) is defined as the number of perinatal deaths per 1,000 total births and is typically reported on an annual basis. It serves as a critical indicator of the quality of healthcare delivery in a given population. However, comparing PNMRs between different regions or countries can be challenging due to variations in definitions, potential biases in registration, and differences in the underlying risk factors of the populations being studied. PNMRs vary significantly worldwide, with rates below 10 per 1,000 births in some developed countries, while rates in developing countries can be more than ten times higher. The WHO has not published recent data on perinatal mortality rates.
